items_missed: No real agenda statement. 'Is now a good time for me to ask you some questions about your move just for more accurate estimate?' gets partial credit for asking permission and naming a purpose, but there was no roadmap (details, then pricing) and no ~10-15 minute timeframe.

Never checked date availability. He knew 'you had your eye on a Tuesday' and quoted the Tuesday rate, but never confirmed the schedule was open for that date — which is also why he had nothing to hold when the customer went to think it over.
What's-included list never given — no gas, truck, taxes, insurance, pads, bands, tools. He named wrapping and disassembly only.

Packing service pricing not explained as same hourly rate plus materials. He priced wardrobe boxes at $15 each and steered off them, but the customer never learned what packing help would actually cost if he wanted it.
No 'no hidden fees' pitch. He covered no deposit, no card info, no penalty fees — but not no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees.
Number of trucks never stated (movers were — 'for a two man team it would be at $190')
No specialty-items question (piano, safe, antiques) — a real gap on a job where the bulk of the inventory is furniture bought at an estate sale
Traffic never named as a variable on a three-stop Houston move
Drive time between the three addresses never called out as a time driver, even though he correctly resequenced the route

Save Your Ass speech not delivered. The clothes-batching advice was money-saving prep, but it was framed as avoiding $15 wardrobe boxes, not as prep = shorter move = lower bill. No consolidation examples beyond clothes (drawers, toys, garden tools, photos off walls), no 'does that make sense?' close.

'Take a carload' tip missed at the exact moment it was handed to him — the customer said 'I might actually be able to move some of that stuff myself. I just need to see.' No reinforcement, no explanation that doing so shortens the clock.
No 60 cents/lb baseline alongside the $2,000 coverage, and the phrasing came out as 'free evaluation coverage' rather than a clean No Worries Damage Coverage explanation
No BOLDED-key-details framing for the confirmation email

No 'any other questions before I let you go?' close, and no business hours given — even though the customer explicitly asked 'what should I do if I'm ready to reserve, just call you back or respond to an email? How should I lock it in?'
No storage-stop, garage/attic/balcony, or moving-stressors question
Customer's name mangled twice mid-call ('Rapha', 'Rough') before landing on Raphael
top_strength: Discovery on a genuinely messy job was the best thing on this call. He opened by recapping the file back to the customer — 'I do have notes here that the move that we're doing for you is a partial move... and then you're moving to a 1600 square foot apartment on the first floor' — which immediately showed he'd prepared. When the customer revealed a surprise third address from an estate sale, Alex didn't get flustered; he resequenced the whole route on the fly with real logic: 'the estate sale, it doesn't make more sense for us to begin to move there since that's where the bulk of the inventory is going to be.' He also gave the customer a box benchmark instead of demanding a count — 'usually we expect to see anywhere from like 25 to 35 boxes. You do not need to have an exact box count there, Rafael, I'm just wondering if that checks out' — and he tied walk distance directly to price so the customer understood why it mattered: 'anything a lot longer than like a thirty second or one minute walk in particular is probably gonna translate to a little bit of a higher estimate.'
coaching_note: Alex, this was a strong call — the fix that would move it most is the close. The customer asked you point blank how to lock it in, and you answered 'I would recommend calling first and then just sending the email.' That handed a warm buyer a homework assignment. You had already asked the right question ('did you want me to go ahead and just create the reservation for you right now?'), so finish it: 'Reservations are completely free and there's no deposit, so let me hold that Tuesday for you right now — if the walk distance changes anything, you just reply to the email and I'll adjust it. Nothing to lose by having the date.' Free reservations are your best closing tool and you used them as a description instead of a reason to book. Second priority: Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee are both missing again, and this call was set up for them — you were already talking about access and arrival at the new apartment, which is exactly where 'a few days before your move we'll email you your mover's photo and info, and if we miss the arrival window we start discounting immediately' belongs. Third, the wardrobe box advice was good instinct but you sold it on materials cost only. Convert it into the full prep speech: 'everything you consolidate before we get there — clothes bagged, drawers cleared, rugs rolled, anything small in your car — shortens the move, and since you're paying by the hour that's straight off your bill.' He told you he might move some things himself; that was your opening and it went by. Last, ask the specialty-items question on estate-sale furniture — antiques and heavy case goods are exactly what blows up an hourly estimate.
phone_presence_notes: Warm and consultative throughout — used the customer's name four times, framed advice personally ('if it was my move'), waved off the background noise with a genuine 'no worries, no worries' when the customer apologized about his daughter, and the customer reciprocated with real enthusiasm ('yeah, that'd be great!', 'Perfect'); mangling the name twice is the only real ding.
